title: Sarla Verma & Ors v. Delhi Transport Corp & Anr
facts: A major judgment by the Supreme Court of India aimed at bringing consistency and uniformity to the calculation of compensation in motor accident claim cases.
The case involved the death of a scientists/engineer in a motor accident caused by a bus owned by Delhi Transport Corporation.
The legal heirs of the deceased challenged the tribunal's award, arguing that the compensation was too low and didn't consider future prospects.
issues: The appropriate multiplier to be applied based on the age of the deceased.
How to calculate the deduction for 'personal and living expenses' of the deceased.
Whether 'future prospects' should be added to the actual income and at what percentage.
analysis_of_law: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988: Specifically dealing with Section 166 (Compensation claims).
Multiplier Method: The standard formula for assessing loss of dependency.
Just Compensation: The constitutional and statutory mandate to provide fair reparation.
precedent_analysis: The Court consolidated various previous conflicting judgments (U.P. State Road Transport Corp v. Trilok Chandra, etc.) to create a standard 'Multiplier Table'.
It established a fixed percentage for future prospects based on whether the deceased was in a permanent salary job.
courts_reasoning: Uniformity in awards is crucial to prevent arbitrariness and ensure similar victims get similar compensation.
Standardized Deduction: 1/3 deduction for bachelors, 1/4 for large families, etc. prevents guesswork by different tribunals.
Standardized Multiplier: The Court provided a definitive list linking age to the multiplier (e.g., 18 for age 21-25).
conclusion: The Supreme Court refined the compensation and provided clear mathematical guidelines that now form the bedrock of Motor Accident Claim Tribunals (MACT).
The award was increased, taking into account future prospects and the correct multiplier.
full_ratio: In motor accident cases, compensation must be calculated using a standardized multiplier method based on age. Future prospects should be added at a fixed rate (e.g., 50% for those below 40 years with permanent jobs), and deductions for personal expenses must follow standardized family-size rules. This ensures 'Just Compensation' for the victims' families.
